title: Keeping the Lights On
paragraphs: An electricity grid has a demanding job: at every moment, the amount of power produced must match the amount being used. For most of the last century, operators managed this by burning more or less fuel in large power stations. Sun and wind are cleaner sources, but they cannot be switched on when needed. Solar panels produce nothing at night, and wind farms slow down when the air is calm.

Engineers are tackling this variability in several ways. Batteries can store extra energy on a sunny afternoon and release it after sunset. Pumped hydro plants use electricity to pump water uphill, then let it flow down through turbines to generate power when it is needed. Long transmission lines help as well, because the wind is rarely calm everywhere at once, so a wider grid can share power between regions. Better weather forecasts allow operators to plan hours or days ahead.

Demand can also become more flexible. Some factories and electric cars can be set to use power when it is plentiful and cheap, instead of when it is scarce. None of these tools is enough on its own, but together they make a grid with a large share of renewables far more reliable. The challenge, in other words, is less about producing clean energy and more about managing it wisely.
